title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle
finding: Transformer attention operates through a keywords-as-cues mechanism where queries encode the retrieval context and keys index memory traces, so retrieval effectiveness depends on how well retrieval cues align with the original encoding context.
example: A transformer retrieves a stored fact only when the query keywords match those present at encoding time [arXiv:2601.20282].
relevance: It directly tests the encoding-specificity (state-dependent retrieval) principle inside a transformer's attention mechanism, showing recall depends on the match between encoding and retrieval cues.
page_title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle

title: Modelling continual learning in humans with Hebbian context gating and exponentially decaying task signals
finding: Slow-updating ('sluggish') task units introduce a switch-cost during training that biases interleaved-training representations toward a joint representation ignoring the contextual cue.
example: A neural network trained to alternate task rules loses accuracy on switch trials because sluggish task units lag the rule change [arXiv:2203.11560].
relevance: It reproduces the human task-switch cost inside a neural network, showing degraded performance when the task rule changes versus repeats.
page_title: Modelling continual learning in humans with Hebbian context gating and exponentially decaying task signals

title: SATBench: Benchmarking the speed-accuracy tradeoff in object recognition by humans and dynamic neural networks
finding: Cascaded dynamic neural networks, using compute (FLOPs) as a reaction-time analog, trace a speed-accuracy tradeoff that matches human accuracy improvements as response urgency increases.
example: A dynamic network allowed more inference steps answers more accurately, trading speed for accuracy like a human under time pressure [arXiv:2206.08427].
relevance: It explicitly measures the speed-accuracy tradeoff in dynamic neural networks under varying response-time budgets, the AI analog of the human effect.
page_title: SATBench: Benchmarking the speed-accuracy tradeoff in object recognition by humans and dynamic neural networks

title: Reawakening knowledge: Anticipatory recovery from catastrophic interference via structured training
finding: When documents are presented cyclically, over-parametrized networks spontaneously recover from catastrophic interference and restore seemingly forgotten knowledge before re-encountering it, an effect that strengthens as the architecture scales.
example: An LLM that had forgotten an earlier document spontaneously recovers its knowledge of it before seeing it again [arXiv:2403.09613].
relevance: It shows an extinguished/overwritten response returning in a neural network, the AI parallel of reinstatement of a previously learned response.
page_title: Reawakening knowledge: Anticipatory recovery from catastrophic interference via structured training

title: Underestimation Bias and Underfitting in Machine Learning
finding: On the Adult dataset the true rate of >50K salaries for females was 11% but an underfitted classifier predicted only 6%, systematically under-associating the rare positive outcome with the minority group, which the paper frames explicitly as the ML analog of illusory correlation.
example: A classifier under-predicts the rare positive class for a minority group, mirroring illusory correlation between a small group and a rare outcome [arXiv:2005.09052].
relevance: The paper explicitly draws the illusory-correlation parallel and shows an ML model perceiving a distorted association between a rare class and a minority (distinctive) group.
page_title: Underestimation Bias and Underfitting in Machine Learning

title: The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems
finding: Both human memory and dense passage retrieval show logarithmic accuracy decline as the number of items associated with a cue (fan) grows, with RAG showing higher interference sensitivity (alpha/sigma = 0.67) than humans (0.41).
example: A dense retriever gets less accurate for a query as more passages are tied to the same cue, interference rising with fan count [arXiv:2606.28327]
relevance: Measures a retrieval cue losing effectiveness as more competing items are associated with it (the fan effect) directly in a RAG / dense-retrieval system.
page_title: The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems

title: Multiple Choice Questions: Reasoning Makes Large Language Models (LLMs) More Self-Confident, Especially When They are Wrong
finding: Models are systematically more confident when they generate reasoning before answering, and this confidence increase is larger when the selected answer is incorrect than when it is correct.
example: An LLM that first generates reasoning rates its own answer as more likely true, most of all when the answer is wrong [arXiv:2501.09775]
relevance: Shows that an LLM generating its own elaboration before committing inflates its confidence in the claim, the model analog of imagining an event raising belief it occurred.
page_title: Multiple Choice Questions: Reasoning Makes Large Language Models (LLMs) More Self-Confident, Especially When They are Wrong

title: Using a Dynamic Neural Field Model to Explore a Direct Collicular Inhibition Account of Inhibition of Return
finding: A dynamic neural field model combining short-term depression and delayed direct collicular inhibition reproduces established inhibition-of-return behaviour, where responding is slowest toward a recently cued location once the cue-target interval exceeds about 200 ms.
example: A neural field model responds slowest toward a location it recently attended once the cue-target gap passes 200 ms [arXiv:1307.5684]
relevance: A computational neural-field model reproduces inhibition of return, slower orienting back to a recently attended spatial location, as an emergent property of its dynamics.
page_title: Using a Dynamic Neural Field Model to Explore a Direct Collicular Inhibition Account of Inhibition of Return

title: Perceptual decision making: Biases in post-error reaction times explained by attractor network dynamics
finding: The attractor neural network exhibits post-error slowing in agreement with empirical data even in the absence of any feedback about the correctness of the decision.
example: An attractor network responds more slowly on the trial right after an error, with no error feedback given [arXiv:1803.00795]
relevance: An attractor neural network model reproduces post-error slowing, slower responses immediately after an error, purely from its intrinsic dynamics.
page_title: Perceptual decision making: Biases in post-error reaction times explained by attractor network dynamics

title: Energy estimates of open-weight large language models across stated food weights: a dose-response evaluation
finding: LLM energy estimates fail to scale with the stated food weight and cluster near a typical serving, overestimating a quarter of the default amount by 47 to 130 percent and underestimating four times the default by 20 to 34 percent.
example: An LLM estimates calories near one typical serving whether told the portion is a quarter or four times the default [arXiv:2611.25976]
relevance: The model treats a typical unit as the appropriate amount, flattening its estimates toward a default serving regardless of the actual stated quantity, an AI instance of unit bias.
page_title: Energy estimates of open-weight large language models across stated food weights: a dose-response evaluation

title: Generative Language Models Exhibit Social Identity Biases
finding: Across 56 large language models, almost all foundational models and some instruction-tuned ones show clear ingroup-positive and outgroup-negative associations, to a degree similar to humans.
example: Prompted with We are, LLMs complete ingroup sentences positively and outgroup sentences negatively [arXiv:2310.15819]
relevance: Demonstrates the ingroup-favouring, outgroup-derogating asymmetry at the heart of the ultimate attribution error directly in language models.
page_title: Generative Language Models Exhibit Social Identity Biases

title: Super-additive Cooperation in Language Model Agents
finding: When language model agents are organized into teams facing intergroup competition, both overall and one-shot cooperation levels rise substantially relative to the individual baseline, a pattern driven by the group-versus-individual distinction.
example: LLM agents placed in competing teams behave very differently in the Prisoners Dilemma than the same agents acting alone [arXiv:2508.15510]
relevance: Shows LLM agents shift their strategic behaviour between individual and intergroup-competitive settings, the hallmark of interindividual-intergroup discontinuity, in a multi-agent AI system.
page_title: Super-additive Cooperation in Language Model Agents

title: Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: LLM retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as semantically related prior key-value updates accumulate, with errors arising from retrieving previously overwritten values.
example: When earlier related items pile up in context, an LLM retrieves a stale overwritten value instead of the current one [arXiv:2506.08184].
relevance: It directly demonstrates that prior, partially overlapping information acts as a cue set that impairs recall of the remaining target items in an LLM, the AI analogue of part-list cueing interference.
page_title: Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length

title: Feature Competition and Its Representational Origins in Vision Language Models: Evidence from the Stroop Paradigm
finding: When text and ink color disagree in a Stroop stimulus, vision-language models preferentially generate the written word rather than reporting the color, because textual cues are more separable in the embedding space.
example: Shown the word GREEN printed in red, most vision-language models answer green, reading the word instead of naming the ink color [arXiv:2610.12650].
relevance: It adapts the classic Stroop paradigm to vision-language models and shows an automatic word-reading response interfering with the required color-naming response, the defining Stroop interference pattern in an AI system.
page_title: Feature Competition and Its Representational Origins in Vision Language Models: Evidence from the Stroop Paradigm

title: How Do LLMs Change Predictions Under Negation?
finding: Under negation, LLMs implement an internal mechanism that suppresses retrieval of the originally expected answer while promoting a favored alternative, though in 37 to 71 percent of cases they still repeat the un-negated answer.
example: Given a negation cue, an LLM internally suppresses the otherwise-expected answer like Madrid and promotes a different candidate [arXiv:2610.09571].
relevance: It shows a learned linguistic cue (negation) signaling that an otherwise-expected outcome should not occur, triggering an internal suppression mechanism in the LLM, the AI analogue of conditioned inhibition.
page_title: How Do LLMs Change Predictions Under Negation?

title: Taming Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Agents via Dialectical Alignment
finding: An LLM agent acting as actor during self-reflection attributes failures to external factors while the same agent as observer attributes identical errors to internal faults, with swapping perspectives triggering this asymmetry in over 20 percent of cases.
example: An LLM agent blames the environment for its own failure but blames another agent's character for the identical error [arXiv:2604.19548].
relevance: It directly benchmarks and demonstrates actor-observer asymmetry in LLM agents, showing situational self-attribution versus dispositional other-attribution for the same failures.
page_title: Taming Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Agents via Dialectical Alignment

title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents
finding: Self-interested LLM agents sustain indirect reciprocity by using gossip-based reputations to help those who have helped others and ostracize defectors, with stronger reasoning yielding more incentive-aligned cooperation.
example: LLM agents help peers who earned good reputations by helping others and withhold aid from known defectors [arXiv:2602.07777].
relevance: It demonstrates the reciprocity norm operating in LLM agents, where receiving or observing help creates pressure to return benefits and defection is punished.
page_title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents

title: In-Context Unlearning: Language Models as Few Shot Unlearners
finding: In-context unlearning, which only supplies forget-instances in the prompt, performs on par with or outperforms methods that update parameters, reducing the model's ability to recall the targeted training instances without changing weights.
example: An LLM told in-context to treat an instance as forgotten drops its ability to recall that training point, matching weight-editing unlearning [arXiv:2310.07579].
relevance: The model is instructed via context to forget selected material and its later accessibility of that material drops, the AI analog of directed forgetting.
page_title: In-Context Unlearning: Language Models as Few Shot Unlearners

title: PALMS: A Computational Implementation for Pavlovian Associative Learning Models' Simulation
finding: In a within-subjects blocking simulation (A trained first, then compounds AB and CD), the pre-trained cue A suppressed learning about B so that B acquired less associative strength than the control cue D.
example: In the PALMS associative-learning simulation a pre-trained cue A blocks learning about a co-presented cue B, which gains less strength than a control cue [arXiv:2602.07519].
relevance: The computational associative-learning system reproduces the Kamin blocking effect, a previously predictive cue preventing learning about a new co-presented cue.
page_title: PALMS: A Computational Implementation for Pavlovian Associative Learning Models' Simulation

title: Reawakening knowledge: Anticipatory recovery from catastrophic interference via structured training
finding: Under cyclic structured training, large models recover performance on documents they had forgotten before those documents are seen again, an anticipatory recovery that emerges as model size increases.
example: A large model regains accuracy on documents it had forgotten during cyclic training, before re-encountering them, with no fresh training on them [arXiv:2403.09613].
relevance: An extinguished (forgotten) response returns in a neural network after time and intervening training, the AI analog of spontaneous recovery.
page_title: Reawakening knowledge: Anticipatory recovery from catastrophic interference via structured training

title: LLM Agents Display Human Biases but Exhibit Distinct Learning Patterns
finding: In the negative-correlation task nearly all tested LLMs chose option B about 50 percent of the time, matching the probability of the higher outcome instead of consistently selecting the objectively better option.
example: In a learning task most LLM agents pick an option at the frequency of its reward, about 50 percent, rather than always choosing the better arm [arXiv:2503.10248].
relevance: LLM agents distribute choices in proportion to outcome frequencies instead of maximizing, the defining signature of probability matching.
page_title: LLM Agents Display Human Biases but Exhibit Distinct Learning Patterns

title: Everyone Conforms, No One Believes: Pluralistic Ignorance in LLM Agent Populations
finding: Across a 100-scenario benchmark, LLM agents publicly conformed to a norm at rates of 64 to 94 percent despite privately opposing that norm, reproducing pluralistic ignorance.
example: LLM agents publicly conform to a norm 64 to 94 percent of the time while privately rejecting it, each assuming the others accept it [arXiv:2608.02758].
relevance: Populations of LLM agents misperceive peers as accepting a norm the majority privately rejects, the AI analog of pluralistic ignorance.
page_title: Everyone Conforms, No One Believes: Pluralistic Ignorance in LLM Agent Populations

title: LLM Task Interference: An Initial Study on the Impact of Task-Switch in Conversational History
finding: Across 5 datasets and 15 task-switches, the authors show that many task-switches in conversational history lead to significant performance degradation on the new target task, even though conversational history usually helps.
example: An LLM keeps part of its processing bound to the prior conversational task and answers the next task worse [arXiv:2402.18216].
relevance: The paper measures residual influence of a previous task left in the conversation, which carries over and degrades the model on the switched-to task, matching attention residue in an AI system.
page_title: LLM Task Interference: An Initial Study on the Impact of Task-Switch in Conversational History

title: Gradient Starvation: A Learning Proclivity in Neural Networks
finding: The paper shows that cross-entropy training captures only a subset of predictive features, where the learned response to one feature is negatively impacted by the strength of another, so a dominant feature suppresses learning of co-occurring ones.
example: A network leans on one salient feature and fails to learn a second predictive feature present in the same inputs [arXiv:2011.09468].
relevance: Gradient starvation is cue competition in a neural network: a more salient cue starves the gradient for another co-presented cue, directly mirroring overshadowing.
page_title: Gradient Starvation: A Learning Proclivity in Neural Networks

title: When Forgotten Facts Return: Relearning-Aware Unlearning of Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Tangent Kernels
finding: The authors find that after approximate unlearning, forgotten facts recover more than in an exact-unlearning baseline once ordinary continued training resumes, tracing the resurfacing to entity embeddings shared with new facts.
example: A fact unlearned from a knowledge-graph model resurfaces once the model is trained further outside the unlearning setting [arXiv:2610.31075].
relevance: This is renewal in an AI system: a response suppressed during unlearning returns when the model is tested or trained outside the unlearning context.
page_title: When Forgotten Facts Return: Relearning-Aware Unlearning of Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Tangent Kernels

title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev
finding: On a zero-risk-bias task, 488 of 500 model responses (97.6%) ranked the zero-risk alternative last only after editing, while in the original framing the model favored eliminating a smaller risk completely over the option with greater total harm reduction.
example: An AI decision model prefers wiping out one risk entirely over an option that reduces more total harm [arXiv:2610.19619].
relevance: The paper directly probes an AI decision model for zero-risk bias and measures the preference for complete elimination of a sub-risk over larger overall reduction.
page_title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev

title: Large Language Models Portray Socially Subordinate Groups as More Homogeneous, Consistent with a Bias Observed in Humans
finding: ChatGPT portrayed African, Asian, and Hispanic Americans as more homogeneous than White Americans, describing racial minority groups with a narrower range of human experience.
example: An LLM writes socially subordinate groups as more internally uniform than dominant groups [arXiv:2401.08495].
relevance: The paper measures outgroup homogeneity bias directly in an LLM's generated text about different social groups.
page_title: Large Language Models Portray Socially Subordinate Groups as More Homogeneous, Consistent with a Bias Observed in Humans
